title: Fourth objection: Christ teaches a grace that brings all who receive it to him (John 6:45)
source_text: XL. Denique si positis omnibus ad agendum praerequisitis, etiam ex parte Dei, non exclusa qualibet gratiae efficacia, semper contingere potest ut voluntas non agat, nulla datur Dei gratia, saltem ordinaria, quam infallibiliter & certo sequatur hominis conversio, & qua qui donantur omnes, nullo excepto, ad Christum veniant. Sed contra Christus ipse docet esse quandam Dei gratiam, quam nemo accipit qui non veniat ad ipsum. Nam quicunque, inquit, audivit & didicit a Patre venit ad me. Joannis capite sexto.
pass_a_gloss: Lastly if, all things prerequisite to acting being posited, even on the part of God, not excluding any efficacy of grace, it can always happen that the will does not act, there is given no grace of God, at least ordinary, which the conversion of man follows infallibly and certainly, and by which all who are gifted, none excepted, come to Christ. But on the contrary Christ himself teaches that there is a certain grace of God, which no one receives who does not come to him. For whoever, he says, has heard and learned from the Father comes to me. John chapter six.
pass_b_english: Finally, if the will can always fail to act even when everything required for acting is in place, on God's side too and with no efficacy of grace whatever left out, then there is no grace of God, at least no ordinary grace, that a person's conversion follows infallibly and surely, and that brings everyone who receives it, without exception, to Christ.
Christ himself teaches the opposite: there is a grace of God that no one receives without coming to him. 'Everyone,' he says, 'who has heard and learned from the Father comes to me' (John 6).

choices.why: Kept as in the preceding locus on free choice in general, so the Roman and Reformed accounts are compared in one vocabulary.
